I love this. Really interested to see how Stoke do this season.

I've always liked Stoke but with the addition of these recent transfers keep thinking of the great phrase of "just because you shot Jesse James, don't make you Jesse James".

Many of them are players who seem to have either faded, were hyped as youngsters and still have a name attached to them despite not really having that talent, or people who have failed at bigger clubs. I happen to know that their chief transfer guru isn't actually a football executive by trade but was a football agent who they employed to get their deals done and they all feel very agenty rather than very scouty if that makes sense?

Will be interesting to watch them this season but cannot help feeling that they're onto a recipe for disaster. Stoke used to have a clear footballing philosophy and identity, not one that everybody agreed with or liked but when you have these it makes the scouting and recruitment process a thousand percent easier. It gives a team cohesion when they're all pulling in the same direction and playing the game in a certain way and getting success out of it. They decided to change this which I thought then was a mistake as I do now, but understand the reasoning behind it from a financial standpoint. However they are starting to enter my head as a potential relegation-shock team just because of their extremely unbalanced squad and confused identity.

Identity is everything in football, the most important thing that you can have. Without it there is no possible success and guaranteed failure. Stoke are attempting to change theirs and I'm not sure that bringing in over-hyped youth prospects no in their early twenties is the way to achieve it. Swansea managed it with no transfer funds as do many other Clubs, it isn't impossible to play a decent and attractive brand of football without buying these players.

Now that you mention it, it does seem more agenty than scouty. I agree Stoke are finding a new identity and it will be good to see how they end up looking. I think Mark Hughes wants to try his own "philosophy", I highly doubt Tony Pulis would have done anything similar. No opinion really if it is good or bad - all depends on how it works out.

True and as you say the proof is ultimately in the pudding, but this then falls under my main objection to Stoke - their identity is based on the whims of their manager and not a decision made by the Club.

A Club needs a fixed identity in how it plays regardless of who is in charge because it's a more sane way of managing the business side in the modern world of football. If you decide to play a certain way, then it's easy not just to identify players but also to identify managers who fit with your philosophy and vision on the game. The main financial benefits come down to the value for money in transfers.

For example, if you work for Barcelona and are in charge of the transfers then you know only to buy Barcelona style players. The manager will of course bring a freshness and their own ideas but the overall plan is always about attacking football using technique and possession based systems; the manager then just works within this framework to implement their own ideas. If you're buying players then it doesn't matter who the manager is because they will all need similar types of players. When players are now going for tens of millions, and a manager's shelf life is about 18 months, spending the Club's money based on a simple identity rather than what the manager wants is just good business. You can't break your transfer record every 18 months, you'll run out of money.

Having a proper footballing identity actually helps with sponsorships and branding too. Stoke's wasn't the most glamorous of course, and the new image they are trying to cultivate will certainly open up different types of sponsors, but having a team who is seen as a tough, working class, hard working group of players could under the right marketing be a perfect fit for many brands out there. Their new identity might be more attractive to sponsors but the problem is that they are now competing for the brands who like that stuff with City, Arsenal, Swansea and others which means they are taking scraps off the large table rather than dominating the smaller one.

Stoke's football reminded me a little of the USMNT or pre-00s Man United in terms of how they set themselves up. They were a team who believed in hard work, physicality and using their athleticism to be successful and they were. When Pulis went and they brought in Hughes it seemed like a logical move; Hughes has always played an attacking form of football based a little more around possession than Stoke did but he still believed in that hard working physical style that he himself used to play. This was an interesting move from Stoke as it was both internal to their identity but could push them on - good appointment.

The players that are getting signed though don't really fit with this ideal. With all due respect to the players mentioned, I look at that squad and see Ibrahim Affelay, Shaqiri, Bojan, and Glen Johnson then added to players already there such as Stephen Ireland and Muniesa and wonder if that is a team that is going to scrap for every ball until they are dead on their feet in a muddy night game in Leicester on a Wednesday December night where they need to defend a 2-1 lead with 10 minutes to go? I'm not sure that it is.

Don't get me wrong, they aren't completely down and out and people like Van Ginkel is certainly the type of player who I think that they should be looking at and they do have a decent amount of hard workers in the team but that's sort of the problem too. A squad that has half people who want to work hard and fight for everything and half players who are a little lax on pressing and defensive responsibilities is a recipe for disaster in terms of resentment that can build after a loss. Ronaldinho had this problem at Barca - when he was the best in the world nobody minded, as soon as his form dipped then other players became irritated and angry at him and ultimately the manager for not working hard enough and not pulling him up on it.

Stoke just seem in a perilous position to me at the moment. There's SO MANY THINGS that could potentially go wrong with what they are doing on numerous different levels and I don't see what the ultimate pay off is.
